hero.prompt: A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom table holding one large blank sheet of poster paper divided into four coloured sections, a tin of coloured markers, a ruler, two closed notebooks and a few small blank yellow and green sticky notes, with sunlight from a window.
hero.alt: A classroom table with a large blank poster divided into four coloured sections, coloured markers, a ruler, two notebooks and sticky notes.

slides.title: Read your own words from Lesson 1
slides.subtitle: Find your Lesson 1 prediction about the cut finger.

blocks.text: A classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes with small gold stars beside some of them.
items: dqb_sticky_notes_board
A friendly flat cartoon of a classroom wall covered in blank yellow and green sticky notes, with three small gold stars stuck beside some notes, and a wooden desk with a pot of pencils in front.
book :: Open your notebook to Lesson 1
eyes :: Find your prediction about the cut finger
thought :: Read it silently. Do not talk.

do: Take the original Driving Question Board poster from the wall. Place it at the front of the room.
Read two or three original wonder questions aloud, word for word. Use a warm, slow voice.
Pause for five full seconds after each question.
Ask learners to open their notebooks to the Lesson 1 entry. Start the timer.
Learners work alone. No materials are needed except notebooks.
say: Here is what Akinyi wrote in Lesson 1. She asked, Why does the body know which cell to send?
Here is what Otieno wrote. He asked, Do all our cells have the same parts?
These were great scientific questions ten lessons ago. Today, let us find out how far our answers have come.
Open your notebook to Lesson 1. Read your own words quietly.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each question is read aloud; 1 minute of silence for re-reading
look_for: Every learner has the Lesson 1 page open within 30 seconds. Scan the whole room.
Learners are reading, not chatting. Note anyone who seems to have no entry.
if_then: If a learner cannot find the entry, say: Look at the first page about the cut finger. Read what you can, then think about what you remember.
If someone starts talking, say: This is quiet time. Read your own words first.
notes.why_this_works: Re-reading their own words makes learners see their own change over time. The wonder questions turn the lesson into finishing a story, not repeating old work.

slides.title: In Lesson 1 I thought… but now I know…
slides.subtitle: Write one sentence. Work alone and in silence.

blocks.text: In Lesson 1 I thought… but now I know…
Finish the sentence in your notebook.
items: Use your own words.
Do not talk until the timer ends.

do: Write the stem on the board: In Lesson 1 I thought… but now I know…
Learners write one sentence in their own notebook, alone.
Circulate quietly. Read two or three sentences over shoulders. Do not collect notebooks.
say: Before we share, write one sentence. Finish this stem: In Lesson 1 I thought… but now I know…
Write without talking. You have a minute and a half.
look_for: Most learners are writing within 15 seconds.
Read 3 to 4 sentences. Note any that mix up cell wall and cell membrane. Remember these for Model Building.
if_then: If a learner is stuck, say: Think of one cell or one part of a cell. What did you not know in Lesson 1 that you know now?
If a learner writes only that cells are important, say: Name one cell and say what it does.
notes.why_this_works: Writing alone first gives every learner something to say. It also shows their own change in thinking, which is more motivating than being told they have learned.
answer_key: In Lesson 1 I thought the skin just closes by itself, but now I know that different cells with different shapes do different jobs, such as platelets that help the blood clot and neutrophils that digest bacteria.

slides.title: THEN and NOW
slides.subtitle: Listen to three sentences. What has changed?

items: THEN :: What we thought in Lesson 1
NOW :: What we know today

blocks.text: Listen for the words that changed.

do: Draw two columns on the chalkboard: THEN and NOW.
Cold-call three learners. Choose learners who showed a wide range of prior knowledge in Lesson 1: one with a simple idea, one with a detailed idea, one in between.
Write the key contrasting words under THEN and NOW as each learner speaks.
No corrections yet. Note any misconception for the Model Building slides.
say: I will choose three of you to read your sentence aloud. Listen for what has changed.
Thank you. I am writing your words on the board so we can see the change.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after the question before choosing a learner
look_for: Each of the three sentence pairs names a specific change, such as specialisation or organelle function.
Note any learner who still mixes up cell wall and cell membrane. Plan to clear this up during the Model Building Phase.
if_then: If a learner says only that cells are important, say: Name one cell or one part of a cell. What does it do?
If the NOW sentence has a wrong idea, do not correct it. Say: Thank you. Let us test that idea on the poster.
notes.why_this_works: Putting Lesson 1 words next to today's words makes learning visible. Not correcting yet keeps learners willing to share honest ideas, and tells you what to clear up later.
answer_key: THEN: The skin just closes by itself. NOW: Different cells with different shapes do different jobs, for example platelets help the blood clot.

slides.title: Our poster model: four zones
slides.subtitle: One group poster. One scientific model.

items: leaf :: Zone A: Plant cell
cow :: Zone B: Animal cell
bandage :: Zone C: Three specialised wound-healing cells
link :: Zone D: Cell organisation hierarchy

blocks.text: Every label must link a structure to a function.

do: Project or draw the blank poster template on the board. Show the four zones: A Plant Cell, B Animal Cell, C Three Specialised Wound-Healing Cells, D Cell Organisation Hierarchy.
Groups of four sit together.
Explain the task. Hold up a marker as you say the key line.
say: Your group will make one scientific model. It is not a decoration. It is not a copy from the textbook.
Your model must use evidence from our practical work, our diagrams and our discussions to explain the wound-healing phenomenon.
Every label on this poster must connect a structure to a function. If you can draw a cell without explaining what it does, your poster is incomplete.
look_for: Groups of four are formed quickly.
Learners can say in their own words what a model needs: evidence and structure-function links.
if_then: If a learner asks if the poster must look beautiful, say: Neat is good, but the science is what counts. Can you explain what each label does?
notes.why_this_works: Saying exactly what a good model must contain, and what it is not, sets a clear standard before learners start. This stops them from drawing for decoration.

slides.title: Silent planning scan
slides.subtitle: Which zones feel strong? Which feel hard?

blocks.text: Write in your notebook. Work alone.
items: I feel most confident about Zone… because…
I feel least confident about Zone… and I will need to use my notes for…

do: Keep the four-zone template visible.
Each learner reads the zone headings silently, then writes the two sentences. Start the timer.
Circulate and read 6 to 8 notebook entries briefly.
Use what you read to give stretch roles. Encourage the learner who is weakest on Zone C to take the main job on that zone, with help from the group.
say: Read the four zone headings silently. Which zone feels strongest for you? Which feels hardest?
Write your two sentences. This helps your group share the work fairly.
look_for: Check 6 to 8 notebooks. Each entry names a zone and gives a reason.
Look for groups where all four learners claimed the same strong zone, or where nobody claimed Zone C. This may mean they are avoiding the hard content.
if_then: If no one in a group has claimed Zone C, say: I notice no one has claimed Zone C. Who in this group is going to take ownership of explaining the platelet and the neutrophil?
If a learner writes only that they are confident about everything, say: Pick the zone where you would most need your notes. Write that one.
notes.why_this_works: Naming their own uncertainty before starting makes learners use their notes more carefully. It also helps fair sharing of work, so hard zones are not avoided.
answer_key: I feel most confident about Zone A because I drew the plant cell in Lesson 4. I feel least confident about Zone C and I will need to use my notes for what each wound-healing cell does.

slides.title: Build your poster: Zones A and B
slides.subtitle: Draw and label plant and animal cells. Add what each part does.
slides.time_note: Building time trimmed from 20:00 to 14:00 across Zones A to D.

items: leaf :: Zone A: label a plant cell. Use at least 8 organelles.
memo :: Write a short function note beside each label.
cow :: Zone B: label an animal cell. Use at least 6 organelles.
question :: Note two structures absent from the plant cell. Explain why their absence matters.

do: Hand out materials to each group of four: A2 poster paper, coloured markers and rulers.
Start the 14-minute timer. It keeps running across the next two slides.
Remind groups to use their cumulative cell model versions and their practical drawings from Lessons 6 and 7.
Circulate with a clipboard. Ask questions, do not correct. Ask: What does that organelle do?
Note for yourself: are structure-function links clear or only hinted at? Photograph posters or sketch key features on your clipboard.
The ARES reading icon is for groups that need to check plant cell structures. Preview it first: it is not an exact match.
Resource link (plain URL for printed copies): see the ARES resource list in the lesson files.
say: Start with Zone A and Zone B. Draw big and clear.
Next to every label, write what that part does. A label with no function is not finished.
I will not tell you what is wrong. I will ask you questions.
notes.wait_time: 7 seconds after each question you ask a group
look_for: Zone A has at least 8 organelles, each with a function phrase.
Zone B has at least 6 organelles and two structures noted as absent from the plant cell.
Check at least one poster from every group. Listen for mix-ups between cell wall and cell membrane.
if_then: If a group has labels but no functions, say: You have drawn it. Now tell me what that part does for the cell.
If a group mixes up cell wall and cell membrane, say: Which one is found in plant cells only? Check your Lesson 4 model.
notes.why_this_works: Asking questions instead of correcting makes learners explain and fix their own mistakes. It also shows you what they really understand.
answer_key: Zone A, plant cell: cell wall (supports and gives shape); cell membrane (controls what enters and leaves); nucleus (controls the cell and holds DNA); chloroplast (photosynthesis); large central vacuole (stores water and keeps the cell firm); mitochondrion (releases energy); endoplasmic reticulum (moves and makes materials); ribosomes (make proteins); Golgi apparatus (packages and sends out proteins).

Zone B, animal cell: cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, mitochondria, ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, each with a function note. Lysosomes (digest bacteria and waste) and centrioles (help cell division) are in animal cells but not in the plant cell. Animal cells have no cell wall, so the cell can change shape. They have no chloroplasts, because animals get food by eating, not photosynthesis.

slides.title: Build your poster: Zone C
slides.subtitle: Show three specialised cells from the healing cut.

blocks.text: What does that feature let the cell do?

items: bandage :: Pick three cells from the healing cut
arrow_right :: Draw an arrow from one feature to one job
eyes :: Show how each cell helps heal the cut

do: Keep circulating with the clipboard. Note: are Zone C cells linked to the wound-healing story, or treated as abstract examples? Are the structure-function links clear or only hinted at?
Use questions, not corrections.

At one group, try this: You have drawn the red blood cell correctly. It is biconcave and has no nucleus. What does having no nucleus allow the red blood cell to do that a nucleated cell cannot do as efficiently? Wait seven seconds.
Learners most often pick platelets, neutrophils or macrophages, and fibroblasts or epidermal cells. Do not say this aloud first; let groups choose.
say: Choose three cells that really took part in healing the cut.
Draw an arrow from one structure to one job.
Tell me: what does that feature let the cell do?
look_for: Each group has three wound-healing cells, each with one clear arrow from a feature to a function.
Check at least one poster per group. Mark groups that only draw cells with no function.
if_then: If a group treats the cells as abstract examples, say: Which part of the healing-cut story does this cell play?
If an arrow is missing, say: Show me the arrow from the shape to the job.
If a group says the cell has that shape just because, say: Why would that shape help the job? What would happen if the cell was round instead?
notes.why_this_works: Requiring an arrow from one feature to one function stops learners from just drawing shapes. It makes them join shape and job, which is the answer to the driving question. A common mistake is thinking shape is for show only.
answer_key: Platelet: small, no nucleus, packed with clotting proteins, so it can stick together quickly to plug the cut.
Neutrophil or macrophage: irregular shape and many lysosomes, so it can engulf and digest bacteria.
Fibroblast: rich in rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, so it can make and release collagen to rebuild tissue. An epidermal cell divides quickly to close the wound surface.

slides.title: Build your poster: Zone D
slides.subtitle: Show the hierarchy from cell to organism.

items: link :: Use the skin as your example
arrow_up :: Go from cell to organism
memo :: One sentence: what is gained at each level?

blocks.text: Not just a list. An explanation.

do: Keep circulating. Look at Zone D on each poster.
Check whether the hierarchy is only a list or an explanatory sequence.
The ARES video icon is for groups that want to review organisation in the human body. Preview first: it is not an exact match. Do not stop the timer.
Resource link (plain URL for printed copies): see the ARES resource list in the lesson files.
say: Zone D is not just a list of five words. Tell the story of what is gained at each level.
What can a tissue do that one cell cannot?
look_for: Zone D goes from cell to organism and each level has a one-sentence gain.
Check at least one poster from every group. Note how many groups show only a list, to address in the Driving Question Board phase.
if_then: If a group lists the levels only, say: What does the tissue do that one cell cannot do alone?
If the order is wrong, say: Which is bigger, the tissue or the organ? Check your Lesson 10 hierarchy.
notes.why_this_works: Asking what is gained at each level turns a memorised list into an explanation of how many small cells make a working body.
answer_key: Epidermal cell: one cell does one small job, such as dividing to close the wound.
Epithelial tissue: many similar cells working together form a continuous covering.
Skin (organ): different tissues together protect the body and keep germs out.
Integumentary system: skin and related parts work together to protect the body.
Whole organism: all the systems together keep the person alive and able to heal.

slides.title: Gallery walk: one glow, one grow
slides.subtitle: Move clockwise. Read the next group's poster.

items: Glow :: Something scientifically accurate and clearly explained
Grow :: One scientific gap or unclear label

blocks.text: Write each on a small sticky note. Stick it on the poster.

do: Each group leaves its poster on the desk. The group then moves clockwise to the next group's poster.
Give out feedback cards and small sticky notes.
Viewers write one glow and one grow and stick them on the poster.
Circulate. Read 6 or more sticky notes. Praise feedback that is scientifically grounded.
If feedback is only about looks, redirect it.
Ask cold-call questions to at least five different learners across groups, for example a learner who wrote a grow note and one who received it.
Photograph posters or sketch key features on your clipboard. Note common gaps, such as Zone D shown only as a list.
say: Move clockwise to the next poster. Read it carefully.
Write one glow and one grow. A glow is something scientifically accurate and clearly explained. A grow is one scientific gap or unclear label.
I can see that this note says the axon on the nerve cell should be longer. That is a strong scientific observation. Well done.
Can you find one piece of scientific evidence on this poster that either supports or challenges what we learned in Lesson 8?
look_for: Every glow and grow names a specific organelle, structure or function. Check at least 6 sticky notes.
Count how many learners you cold-called. You need at least five.
if_then: If feedback is only about neatness, say: Can you find one piece of scientific evidence on this poster that either supports or challenges what we learned in Lesson 8?
If a learner cannot think of a grow, say: Pick one label. Does it say what the part does?
notes.why_this_works: Writing a specific glow and grow turns peer review into scientific communication. Using sticky notes on the poster means every group gets real feedback to use.
answer_key: Glow: The neutrophil shows many lysosomes with an arrow to digesting bacteria. This is accurate and clear.
Grow: Zone D lists the levels but does not say what is gained at each level.

slides.title: Read your feedback
slides.subtitle: Do you agree with the grow note? Fix one label.
slides.time_note: Reading and revising trimmed from 2:00 plus 1:00 to 1:00 in total.

items: eyes :: Read the sticky notes on your poster
speech :: Do we agree with this grow note?
pencil :: Revise one label before we close the board

do: Groups return to their own posters.
They read the sticky notes, talk quickly about whether they agree with the grow note, and make one quick revision.
Circulate and listen to two or three groups.
say: Go back to your own poster. Read the notes your peers left.
Do we agree with this grow note? Can we fix one label before the Driving Question Board closure?
look_for: Each group makes at least one revision that adds a function or fixes a label.
Listen to 2 or 3 groups. Do they discuss the science or only agree quickly?
if_then: If a group says they have nothing to change, say: Read the grow note again. What would make that label clearer?
notes.why_this_works: Using peer feedback straight away shows learners that feedback is for improving their model, not just for a mark.
answer_key: Grow note said the label was unclear. Revised label: Lysosomes: digest bacteria that the neutrophil engulfs.

slides.title: Driving Question Board: how far have we come?
slides.subtitle: Vote on each wonder question from Lesson 1.

items: green_circle :: ANSWERED: we have strong evidence
yellow_circle :: PARTIALLY ANSWERED: some evidence, gaps remain
blue_circle :: BEYOND THIS UNIT: needs further study

do: Take the original Driving Question Board. Prepare green, yellow and blue sticky notes.
Read each Lesson 1 wonder question slowly and clearly. Ask the learner who wrote it to read it, if possible.
Ask: Who wrote this? Do you feel it has been answered by our work across this unit?
Ask the class: Does anyone want to add to that?
Class vote by show of hands: ANSWERED, PARTIALLY ANSWERED or BEYOND THIS UNIT.
Put a green, yellow or blue sticky note on the question to match the vote.
Note any question with strong disagreement to revisit in Lesson 12.
Keep a brisk pace. Use a calm, ceremonial tone.
say: This is an important moment. We are going back to the questions you asked in Lesson 1.
Who wrote this? Can you tell us, do you feel this question has been answered by the work we have done?
Does anyone want to add to that?
We are not saying BEYOND THIS UNIT because the question is unimportant. We are saying it because great science always creates new questions, and that is a sign of a deep thinker.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each learner response, before taking another voice
look_for: Learners give evidence from our lessons, our practical work or our posters when they vote. Listen to at least 6 learners.
Watch for learners who vote with the crowd and cannot give a reason.
if_then: If a learner votes ANSWERED but cannot give a reason, say: What evidence from our lessons, our practical work, or our posters supports that answer?
If the class cannot agree, say: Let us mark this one for Lesson 12. What evidence would help us decide?
notes.why_this_works: Voting with evidence shows learners the difference between knowing something and just agreeing. Colour labels make clear what the class knows, what is half-known and what is still open.
answer_key: Typical outcomes: questions about what organelles do are ANSWERED.
Questions about why some people heal faster than others may be PARTIALLY ANSWERED.
Questions about how DNA controls which genes are used in different cells are BEYOND THIS UNIT.

slides.title: Answer the driving question together
slides.subtitle: Build one answer, one sentence at a time.

blocks.text: Why do cells in our body look so different from each other, and how does the shape of a cell determine the job it can do?

items: thinking :: Learner 1: cell shape
puzzle :: Learner 2: organelle function
star :: Learner 3: specialisation
bandage :: Learner 4: the healing cut

do: Read the driving question aloud.
Cold-call at least four learners. Choose learners who gave clear answers earlier, and one who has been quiet.
Write the answer on the chalkboard sentence by sentence. Learner 1 adds cell shape, Learner 2 organelle function, Learner 3 specialisation, Learner 4 links to wound healing.
Write down any weak responses to plan the Lesson 12 cold-calls.
say: Let us build one answer together. Each of you adds one sentence to the one before.
Learner 1, start with the shape of cells. Learner 2, add what the parts inside do.
Learner 3, tell us about specialisation. Learner 4, bring us back to the cut finger.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after each question before calling a learner
look_for: Each of the four sentences adds something new and builds on the one before.
Listen for a link between a structural feature and a job, and for the healing cut.
if_then: If a learner repeats the last sentence, say: Add something new. Which cell would you use as an example?
If a learner gives a vague answer, say: Which part of the cell, and what does it do?
notes.why_this_works: Building one answer across several voices shows that scientific reasoning is shared. Each learner has a small, clear job, so more learners take part.
answer_key: Cells look different because their shapes and parts fit their jobs. Organelles do different tasks, such as lysosomes digesting bacteria. Specialised cells have the features they need, such as platelets that clot blood. In the healing cut, platelets, neutrophils and fibroblasts each do a different job, so the finger heals.

slides.title: My cell model: Version 4
slides.subtitle: Write a short synthesis on a fresh page in your notebook.

blocks.text: A girl smiling and holding up one finger with a neat plaster on it, beside a chopping board with sliced onions.
items: amina_healing_finger

A friendly flat cartoon of one teenage girl in a school uniform smiling and holding up one hand with a neat plaster on her finger, standing beside a kitchen table with a wooden chopping board of sliced onions.
My cell model started in Lesson 1 as a simple sketch. Today, Version 4 of my model shows…
The most important connection I now understand is between… and… because…
This connects back to the wound-healing phenomenon because…

do: Write the three sentence starters on the board.
Learners open their notebooks to a fresh page and write for the timed period, alone.
Circulate and read entries over shoulders. Check at least 8 notebooks. Pick the two most articulate and the two most incomplete responses.
Clear up any cell wall and cell membrane mix-ups you noted earlier by asking questions.
say: Open to a fresh page. Finish these three sentences about your own model.
Be specific. Name a part of a cell, say what it does, and link it to the cut finger.
Write without talking.
look_for: Each entry names a specific structure, links it to a specific function, and connects to wound healing. Check at least 8 notebooks.
Note entries that stay general, such as cells are important because they do things in the body.
if_then: If an entry is abstract, give a quiet verbal prompt: Add one specific example. Which cell, and which part?
If a learner copies from the poster, say: Put it in your own words. What does it mean for the cut finger?
notes.why_this_works: Writing the structure, function and phenomenon chain in their own words stops learners from simply copying the poster. It checks real understanding. A common mistake is thinking shape is only decoration, and this prompt makes learners link shape to function.
answer_key: My cell model started in Lesson 1 as a simple sketch. Today, Version 4 of my model shows plant and animal cells, three wound-healing cells and the hierarchy from cell to organism. The most important connection I now understand is between lysosomes in neutrophils and killing bacteria, because lysosomes digest what the cell engulfs. This connects back to the wound-healing phenomenon because neutrophils clear bacteria so the cut does not get infected.

slides.title: Next: back to the cut finger
slides.subtitle: Two of you will share. Then we look ahead.

blocks.text: In Lesson 1 you wondered why cells look different. Now you can explain it.

items: speech :: Two learners share their entries
book :: Keep your notebook. We do not collect it today.
trophy :: Your posters stay up for Lesson 12

do: Cold-call the two learners with the clearest entries. This shows the level of detail needed in Lesson 12 and in the sub-strand assessment.
Do not collect notebooks. Learners need them to prepare overnight.
Tell groups their posters stay displayed for Lesson 12.
Point to the Driving Question Board for the closing words.
say: Thank you. That is the level of detail I want to hear tomorrow.

In Lesson 1 you wondered why cells look different. Today your posters and your words show you can now explain it, using evidence and the language of science. That is what it means to think like a biologist.
Tomorrow we return one final time to the cut finger. You will explain it completely, cell by cell, using everything in your notebook and on your poster. Come ready.
Every green question up there is something your class figured out together. Be proud of it.
notes.wait_time: 5 seconds after asking for volunteers, then cold-call
look_for: The two shared entries name a structure, a function and the healing cut.
Remember which learners gave clear answers and which gave vague ones. Use this to plan Lesson 12 cold-calling.
if_then: If a shared entry is vague, say: Add one specific example. Which cell and which part?
If a learner is shy about sharing, say: Read just your last sentence. We would like to hear it.
notes.why_this_works: Looking forward to the next lesson keeps the class moving and shows this lesson is a step, not the end. Choosing clear examples shows the standard without shaming weaker writers.

build_log.sow_says: Stated times: re-reading ninety seconds, writing two minutes, planning scan three minutes, poster construction approximately twenty minutes, gallery walk four minutes, reading feedback two minutes plus one minute revising, individual writing three minutes in the final five minutes. Teacher talk, DQB voting and cold-calls have no stated times.
build_log.deck_does: Fits 40 minutes: unit map 1, goals 1, Predict 5, Observe 3, Explain 18, Driving Question Board 6, Model Building 4, summary 2. No activity is cut. Estimated SoW phase times about 8, 5, 24, 10 and 5 minutes (about 52 in all), trimmed to the new times.
build_log.why: The SoW activities plus teacher talk cannot fit 40 minutes. Some phases lost more than a quarter because the lesson overruns (Predict, Observe and DQB lose more). Please check the SoW times.

build_log.slide: Several slides: Read your own words from Lesson 1; In Lesson 1 I thought… but now I know…; Silent planning scan; Build your poster: Zones A and B; Read your feedback; My cell model: Version 4
build_log.sow_says: Re-reading 90 seconds; writing 2 minutes; planning scan 3 minutes; construction about 20 minutes; reading feedback 2 minutes then revision 1 minute; individual writing 3 minutes; gallery walk 4 minutes.
build_log.deck_does: Timers: re-reading 1:00; writing 1:30; scan 2:00; building 14:00 (shown as 14:00, 9:00 and 4:00 across three slides); reading and revising 1:00 together; writing 2:30. Gallery walk stays at 4:00.
build_log.why: Timers have to fit inside the trimmed slide minutes.

build_log.sow_says: DQB phase: each original wonder question is read, voted on and relabelled with a coloured note, and at least four learners build an answer to the driving question.
build_log.deck_does: Allows 3 minutes for the voting and 2 minutes for the combined answer, with a brisk pace noted for the teacher. No question or activity is cut.
build_log.why: The number of questions on the DQB is not known. Even a short list of questions plus four cold-calls is unlikely to fit 5 minutes. SoW owner to confirm whether this lesson should be an 80-minute double lesson.

build_log.sow_says: Observe teacher moves: 'sets a visible timer for twenty minutes of construction time'. Explain learner experience: 'Groups spend approximately twenty minutes constructing their posters.'
build_log.deck_does: Puts the construction timer on the first Explain slide (Build your poster: Zones A and B), after the planning scan in Observe.
build_log.why: The same 20 minutes is placed in two phases in the SoW, so it is counted once. The construction is a model-building activity, which fits with the Explain phase as the SoW itself places it.

build_log.sow_says: My cell model started in Lesson 1 as a simple sketch. Today, Version 4 of my model shows…
build_log.deck_does: Keeps 'Version 4' as written.
build_log.why: The storyline calls the Lesson 10 model Version 4, so the Lesson 11 revision would be a later version. Check numbering with the SoW owner.

build_log.slide: Read your own words from Lesson 1
build_log.sow_says: Overview: 'revisiting their Lesson 1 sticky-note predictions, held on the Driving Question Board'. Framework: learners find their Lesson 1 prediction in their science notebooks.
build_log.deck_does: Learners re-read their notebook prediction. The Driving Question Board wonder questions are read aloud by the teacher.
build_log.why: The Lesson 1 predictions were written in notebooks, and sticky notes on the board were notice and wonder notes. The overview and framework do not agree.

build_log.slide: Build your poster: Zones A and B
build_log.sow_says: Zone B requires a fully labelled animal cell with at least six organelles, 'noting two structures absent from the plant cell and explaining why their absence matters'.
build_log.deck_does: Slide uses the SoW wording. Answer key gives lysosomes and centrioles as animal-only structures, and also notes that animal cells lack a cell wall and chloroplasts.
build_log.why: It is unclear whether 'absent from the plant cell' means structures only in animal cells (lysosomes, centrioles) or structures the animal cell lacks (for example cell wall, chloroplasts). 'Their absence' suggests the second. Teacher checker to decide.

build_log.sow_says: platelets (small, no nucleus, packed with clotting proteins — able to aggregate rapidly)
build_log.deck_does: Keeps the SoW wording in the answer key; platelets are not named on the student slide.
build_log.why: Platelets are fragments of larger cells (megakaryocytes), not whole cells. Calling them specialised cells may need a note.

build_log.sow_says: Unit phenomenon: 'A Form 1 student in Nairobi cuts their finger'.
build_log.deck_does: Does not use 'Form 1' on any slide. Refers to the cut finger or the wound-healing phenomenon.

lesson_oneliner: Put the cell story together and explain how the cut finger heals.
purpose: Learners bring together everything they know about cell structure, specialisation and organisation in one group poster-model.
The poster explains the healing cut from cell to organism. Every label must link a structure to a function.
Learners compare their Lesson 1 ideas with what they know now. They see their own thinking change.
The Driving Question Board is reviewed. Every Lesson 1 wonder question is marked ANSWERED, PARTIALLY ANSWERED or BEYOND THIS UNIT.
This lesson is the synthesis step before the final consolidation and assessment in Lesson 12.
before_class: Find the original Driving Question Board poster from Lesson 1. Pick two or three wonder questions to read aloud, word for word.
Prepare green, yellow and blue sticky notes for relabelling the wonder questions.
Count out per group of four: A2 poster paper, coloured markers and rulers.
Prepare feedback cards and small sticky notes for the gallery walk.
Draw or project the blank four-zone poster template: Zone A Plant Cell, Zone B Animal Cell, Zone C Three Specialised Wound-Healing Cells, Zone D Cell Organisation Hierarchy.
Make groups of four. Arrange desks so groups can move clockwise without collisions.
Check that learners can bring their notebooks with the Lesson 1 entry, their cumulative model versions, and their Lesson 6 and 7 drawings.
Make a cold-call list: three for THEN and NOW, at least five during the gallery walk, four for the driving question, two for the closing share.
Prepare a clipboard for notes. Preview the two ARES icons offline before class.
do_not_show: Do not show or hand out labelled plant cell or animal cell diagrams, or sample posters, before groups have built their own Zones A to D.
Do not show the Summary Table slide until learners have finished their own Version 4 writing.
Do not read out the model answers in these notes before learners have written their own.
so_far: You have studied the healing cut, plant and animal cells, specialised cells and how cells are organised.
goals: Describe plant and animal cells in one labelled model.
Explain how the structure of specialised cells fits their jobs.
Compare what you thought in Lesson 1 with what you know now.

key_words.definition: A drawing or diagram that explains how something works.
What we see, measure or learn that supports an idea.
The shape and parts of a cell.
The job that a part or a cell does.
A cell with a shape and parts that suit one job.
An order from the smallest level to the biggest level.

summary.observe_prompt: What did your group put on its poster, and what did the gallery walk feedback show?
summary.learn_prompt: What do plant and animal cells share, and how do they differ?
summary.explain_prompt: How do structure, function and organisation explain the healing cut?
summary.next_lesson: We return to the cut finger and explain it fully, cell by cell.
summary.answer_observe: In this lesson I put my cell knowledge into a four-zone poster model. In the gallery walk, feedback was most useful when it named a specific organelle and its function. In the Driving Question Board vote, we talked about which Lesson 1 questions were answered and which were only partly answered.
summary.answer_learn: I learned that plant and animal cells share core organelles, but only plant cells have a cell wall, a large central vacuole and chloroplasts. Specialised cells in healing have features that suit their jobs. The levels from cell to organism show how small cell jobs add up to a big response such as healing.
summary.answer_explain: My model links organelle structure to cell function, then to tissue and organ roles, then to the whole body. In the healing cut, platelets, neutrophils and fibroblasts each have features that suit their jobs, so together the finger heals. This answers why cells look so different and how shape decides the job a cell can do.
reflection: Did all four zones of the poster get about the same depth, or did groups spend too long on Zones A and B and give Zone C only a little?
Was the glow and grow feedback about science, or mostly about looks?
Could learners explain the link from structure to function to the healing cut aloud as well as in writing?
Are any Driving Question Board questions still unresolved? Is that a gap in the unit, or are they beyond Grade 10?
Which learners gave clear cold-call answers and which gave vague ones? How will you support the vague ones in Lesson 12?

notes.why_this_works: Writing what they observed, learned and can now explain helps learners pull the lesson together. It also gives them a first draft for the Lesson 12 explanation of the cut finger.

Tomorrow, in Lesson 12, we return to the cut finger and explain it fully.
unit_map_notes.why_this_works: Showing where the lesson sits in the unit helps learners see today as the step that joins all the earlier lessons.

do: Read the three goals aloud, one at a time.
Say each key word and its plain meaning. Do not ask learners to copy them.
Ask learners to look for these words during the poster task.
say: By the end of today you can describe plant and animal cells, explain how specialised cells fit their jobs, and compare your thinking with Lesson 1.
These key words are tools for today: model, evidence, structure, function, specialised cell and hierarchy.
Listen for them as we work.
goals_notes.why_this_works: Short, clear goals tell learners what success looks like. Meeting the key words before the task lets them use the words in their own explanations.
